title: Choose Building Blocks by Their Guarantees
summary: Give every box in your diagram a job: connect the requirement, the technology that meets it and the pattern that makes it work.
body:
Think in three layers: a concept explains the constraint, a technology gives you a mechanism, and a pattern combines mechanisms to solve a recurring problem. A product name is useful only when you can explain what it guarantees.

## Start from a request

Take a familiar flow: accept an order, then send a receipt. The order needs a durable record. Email is slower and can fail independently. Now you have a reason for a transactional database and an asynchronous worker—not yet for sharding or a globally replicated log.

## Match a component to its job

| Building block | A reason to use it | A question you must answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relational database | Transactions, constraints and flexible queries | What must commit atomically? Which indexes support reads? |
| Key-value or document store | Access patterns that map naturally to keys or documents | What consistency, transaction and query guarantees are actually available? |
| Cache | Avoid repeated expensive reads | What is the source of truth, and how stale may a response be? |
| Queue or event log | Decouple producers from processing | Can messages repeat or arrive out of order? How do consumers recover? |
| Object storage | Store large files separately from metadata | How are access, upload completion and retention controlled? |
| Search index | Support text search or specialized retrieval | How does the index catch up with the authoritative data? |
| Load balancer | Route requests across healthy instances | What happens to sessions and in-flight work when an instance fails? |

These are useful categories, not hard boundaries. Some document stores support transactions; some relational databases scale horizontally. Check the workload and required guarantees before choosing a specific system.

## Compose mechanisms into patterns

A cache-aside read tries the cache, falls back to the database and fills the cache. An asynchronous path stores work durably before a worker acts. An idempotent consumer recognizes repeated delivery before applying an effect. Each pattern brings state to track and failures to handle.

For the receipt, saving an order and publishing a message are two writes that can fail separately. A transactional outbox records the order and its event in one database transaction; a dispatcher forwards the event later. Forwarding can repeat, so the consumer still needs duplicate handling. Explain this flow rather than stopping at the name "outbox."

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|"POST /orders"| API["Order API"]
    API -->|"one transaction"| DB[("orders + outbox rows")]
    DB --> RL["Outbox relay"]
    RL --> Q[["Order events"]]
    Q --> W["Receipt worker"]
    W -->|"skip if seen"| SEEN[("Processed event IDs")]
    W --> EM["Email provider"]
```

The order and event commit together: neither can commit without the other in this transaction. The relay publishes outbox rows and marks them sent. A crash between those steps causes another publish, so the worker tracks event IDs. For an external email call, that record alone is not enough: marking it done before sending can lose a receipt; marking it afterwards can duplicate one. Persist the send intent, reuse the event ID with the provider's idempotency contract where supported, and reconcile uncertain outcomes. Without provider support, state the remaining delivery tradeoff.

## Scale only when a bottleneck justifies it

Ask what is under pressure: reads, writes, data size, one hot key or an external dependency? A read replica cannot fix a write bottleneck. A cache cannot enforce a rule using stale data. More queue workers can overwhelm a provider unless concurrency is bounded.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["Measured bottleneck"] --> R["Repeated reads"]
    P --> WR["Write volume or data size"]
    P --> BL["Large files"]
    P --> SR["Text or geo search"]
    P --> HK["One hot key"]
    P --> SD["Slow dependency"]
    R --> R2["Cache or read replicas"]
    WR --> W2["Batching or partitioning"]
    BL --> B2["Object storage and CDN"]
    SR --> S2["Search index fed by change events"]
    HK --> H2["Split key, cache, or limit"]
    SD --> D2["Queue with bounded workers"]
```

Match the fix to the pressure. Replicas do not add write capacity; simply adding partitions does not spread one hot key. Name the pressure, choose the block, then explain its new failure mode: cache staleness, replica lag, index lag or queue backlog.

## Try it

Design the first version of a file-sharing service. Give file bytes, metadata and access permissions a home. Walk through one upload and one download. Add a search index only if search is required, and explain what users see before it catches up.

## Continue learning

Start with Foundations for vocabulary and Data & Storage for persistence guarantees, then explore the reliability and distributed modules for failure handling. Try a full case study yourself before reading its reference discussion.

## Further reading

- [microservices.io: Transactional outbox](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/transactional-outbox.html) describes the outbox pattern and its relay options.
- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications](https://dataintensive.net/) explains the guarantees behind databases, logs and derived data systems.
keyTakeaways: Choose mechanisms to satisfy requirements, not to maximize the number of technologies in a diagram.
Explain transactions, consistency, delivery and recovery guarantees explicitly.
A database plus a queue creates a dual-write problem; an outbox still requires duplicate handling.
Identify the bottleneck before selecting a scaling technique.
